Title: RCD protection for socket-outlets
Our paraphrase: Socket-outlets rated up to 32 A on AC final circuits need additional protection from an RCD with a rated trip current of 30 mA or less. Title: Main protective bonding
Our paraphrase: Extraneous metal that enters the building, such as gas and water service pipes and structural steel, is bonded to the main earthing terminal so touch voltages stay low if a fault occurs.

Our paraphrase: The size of the main bonding conductor follows from the size of the supply neutral or earthing conductor. The usual copper minimum is 6 mm2 and the maximum 25 mm2, and 10 mm2 is common on PME supplies. The table that fixes the sizes is copyrighted and is not reproduced.

Title: Circuit protective conductor size
Our paraphrase: Size the circuit protective conductor (cpc) either by the adiabatic equation, which limits heating during a fault, or from a simplified table that relates it to the line conductor size. The table is copyrighted and is not reproduced.

Title: Earthing conductor and main earthing terminal
Our paraphrase: The earthing conductor runs from the main earthing terminal to the earth electrode or the supplier's earth terminal. It must be sized, protected against corrosion and mechanical damage, and connected at the main earthing terminal.

Title: Earth electrodes for TT systems
Our paraphrase: A TT installation relies on its own earth electrode (a rod or pipe, tape or wire, or plate) and on RCD protection. The electrode resistance multiplied by the RCD trip current must stay at or below 50 V.

Title: Isolation and switching, and the main switch
Our paraphrase: Every installation can be isolated by a main switch at its origin that opens all live conductors, and each circuit or item of equipment has isolation and switching suited to its use. The main switch must be accessible and isolators can be secured against being switched on by mistake.

Title: Workmanship and materials

Title: Consumer unit enclosure
Our paraphrase: In domestic premises, consumer units and similar boards follow BS EN 61439-3 and are either made of non-combustible material (steel counts) or housed in a non-combustible cabinet.

Title: Earthing arrangements: TN-S, TN-C-S and TT
Our paraphrase: The supply's earthing arrangement decides how a fault is cleared. TN-S: the supplier provides a separate earth. TN-C-S (also called PME): the supplier combines neutral and earth, so the installation's earth comes from the neutral. TT: the installation uses its own earth electrode, so RCD protection is needed to clear faults.

Title: Supplementary bonding in bathrooms
Our paraphrase: Extra bonding between metal parts in a room with a bath or shower can be left out only if all circuits there have RCD protection and automatic disconnection, and all incoming metal is already main-bonded.

Title: Overload protection and cable coordination
Our paraphrase: The protective device rating must sit between the circuit's design current and the cable's current-carrying capacity (Ib <= In <= Iz), and the device's guaranteed tripping current must not exceed 1.45 times the cable capacity.

Title: Short-circuit protection
Our paraphrase: The device must clear a short circuit before the cable overheats: the cable's heat-withstand limit must be higher than the let-through energy of the device.

Title: Dividing an installation into circuits
Our paraphrase: The installation is divided into several circuits so that a fault affects as little as possible, safe maintenance is possible and nuisance tripping is limited. The UK has no fixed list of dedicated circuits like the NEC's.

Title: Maximum demand
Our paraphrase: The designer assesses the maximum demand, with diversity, to size the supply and the conductors. The standard diversity tables are in IET guidance, not in BS 7671 itself.

Title: Current-carrying capacity and derating
Our paraphrase: A cable's current-carrying capacity depends on how it is installed, the ambient temperature, grouping with other circuits and thermal insulation. The capacity tables are in Appendix 4 and are copyrighted, so the figures are not reproduced.

Our paraphrase: Voltage drop from the origin of the installation to the load must stay within the limits in Appendix 12, commonly given as 3 percent for lighting and 5 percent for other circuits on a 230 V public supply.

Title: Conductor colours
Our paraphrase: Single-phase installations use brown for the line, blue for the neutral and green-and-yellow for the circuit protective conductor; three-phase installations use brown, black and grey for the lines.

Title: Cables concealed in walls and partitions
Our paraphrase: A cable concealed less than 50 mm below a wall surface must run in a safe zone (vertical and horizontal runs tied to accessories and corners) and have 30 mA RCD protection, unless it has another protection listed in 522.6.204.

Title: Alternatives to RCD protection for concealed cables
Our paraphrase: A concealed cable can avoid the RCD requirement if it has an earthed metal sheath or earthed conduit or trunking, is protected against nails and screws by its construction or an earthed barrier, or is a SELV or PELV circuit.

Title: Bathrooms and shower rooms
Our paraphrase: A room with a bath or shower is divided into zones. Zone 0 is inside the bath or shower tray, zone 1 is above it up to 2.25 m, and zone 2 extends 0.6 m beyond zone 1. Only very low voltage (SELV) equipment is allowed in zone 0. Socket-outlets other than shaver units are not allowed in zones 0 to 2, and IP ratings and RCD protection apply across the zones.

Title: Electric vehicle charging points
Our paraphrase: Each charging point needs 30 mA RCD protection plus protection against residual direct current (a Type B RCD, or a Type A or F RCD with a 6 mA residual direct current detecting device). Special rules limit the use of a PME earth for outdoor charging points. Amendment 4 reportedly changes the residual direct current wording, so the current text needs checking.

Title: Accessibility and maintenance
